section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historians continue to debate the meaning of Jacksonian democracy. Some argue that the age of Jackson marked a genuine expansion of political power to ordinary white men: universal white male suffrage, the rotation of officeholders, and a president who claimed to speak directly for the people against entrenched elites. Others counter that Jacksonian democracy was narrow and coercive: it celebrated the 'common man' while tightening racial exclusion, removing Native peoples, and defending slavery - a democracy for white men built on the subjugation of others.
questions.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about the nature of Jacksonian democracy.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific development of the period 1820 to 1848 could be used to support the passage's claim that Jacksonian democracy broadened political participation.
C. Briefly explain how ONE specific development of the same period could be used to challenge the passage's suggestion that Jacksonian democracy was genuinely democratic.
exemplar: The passage argues that Jacksonian democracy was a contradictory achievement: it genuinely broadened political participation for ordinary white men while simultaneously deepening racial exclusion and coercion.
The expansion of white male suffrage - as property qualifications fell away and voter turnout surged to about 80 percent by 1840 - supports the passage's claim of broader political participation.

The forced removal of the Cherokee and other southeastern nations on the Trail of Tears (1838-1839), carried out under Jackson's removal policy, challenges any claim that Jacksonian democracy was genuinely democratic.

questions.stimulus_text:
"We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James... Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation..."
—Mayflower Compact, 1620
parts: A. Briefly explain what the signers of the Mayflower Compact intended to accomplish.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason English colonies in the New World proved successful.
C. Briefly explain ONE advantage enjoyed by the rival French colonies.
exemplar: The signers intended to create a legitimate civil government even though they had landed outside the bounds of their Virginia charter. By 'covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick,' they agreed to make and obey laws for the colony's 'better Ordering and Preservation.'

One reason English colonies succeeded was their early practice of self-government. Virginia's House of Burgesses (1619) gave settlers a voice in their affairs, drawing more migrants and defusing conflict with authority.

The French enjoyed the advantage of strong Native alliances. Because their fur-trade empire depended on Native hunters and middlemen, the French built partnerships rather than seizing farmland, sparing them the costly wars that drained English colonies.

questions.stimulus_text: The map shows the routes of Christopher Columbus's four voyages to the Americas, 1492-1503. The first voyage (1492-1493) sails from Spain to the Bahamas and the northern coast of Hispaniola. The second (1493-1496) reaches Dominica and explores the Caribbean islands. The third (1498-1500) sails farther south, touching the coast of present-day Venezuela in South America. The fourth (1502-1504) explores the coast of Central America. Outward and homeward tracks are numbered by voyage.
questions.attribution: Described from the map 'The Four Voyages of Christopher Columbus, 1492-1503.'
parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE pattern in European exploration shown by the routes on the map.
B. Briefly explain ONE way Columbus's voyages transformed life for Native Americans.
C. Briefly explain ONE way Columbus's voyages transformed life for Europeans.
exemplar: The map shows Columbus sailing steadily farther south and west with each voyage: the first lands in the Bahamas, while the third and fourth reach the South American mainland and Central America. The pattern reveals a deliberate, crown-sponsored program of exploration pushing deeper into unknown territory rather than a single accidental landfall.

For Native Americans the voyages were catastrophic. European diseases such as smallpox, to which Native peoples had no immunity, ravaged populations across the Caribbean and the mainland. The Spanish also imposed the encomienda system, forcing Native peoples into plantation labor and wiping out communities that resisted.

For Europeans the voyages opened access to the wealth of a new hemisphere. Silver and gold from Central and South America flowed to Spain, and new crops — potatoes, maize, tobacco — entered European diets and agriculture. The voyages also launched the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, diseases, and ideas that permanently altered both continents.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which American participation in World War I fostered political, economic, and social change in the United States in the period from 1915 to 1935.

documents.text: Whoever, when the United States is at war, shall willfully make or convey false reports or false statements with intent to interfere with the operation or success of the military or naval forces of the United States . . . or shall willfully obstruct . . . the recruiting or enlistment service of the United States, or . . . shall willfully utter, print, write, or publish any disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the form of government of the United States, or the Constitution of the United States, or the military or naval forces of the United States . . . shall be punished.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Congress, acting at the Wilson administration's request weeks after the U.S. entered the war. Purpose: to criminalize interference with the war effort, broadly defined to include 'disloyal' speech about the government. Audience: federal prosecutors and the public. Why it matters: the statute is the legal engine of wartime suppression of dissent — the political change the war produced at its most coercive.

documents.text: [Descriptive entry — no excerpted text in the source: an open letter from Black editor William Charles Morris arguing that President Wilson's crusade to 'make the world safe for democracy' required making America safe for democracy for Black Americans.]
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Morris, a Black newspaper editor, writing as Wilson proclaimed a war to make the world safe for democracy. Purpose: to turn Wilson's war rhetoric back on the nation — demanding democracy at home for Black Americans facing lynching, disfranchisement, and segregation. Audience: Black readers and, by its open-letter form, the president himself. Why it matters: the document shows how the war's democratic ideals became a lever for Black protest, linking wartime service to claims for civil rights. (The book reprints the title without excerpted text; this entry describes the editorial's argument from its title and historical context rather than quoting it.)

documents.text: Adolph Anton, residing at 1100 Sixth Avenue West, was taken from his home at about nine o'clock last night by a party of five or six who came to the house in an auto, carried to a spot on the Beaser Avenue road known as the Chequamego Ice Company's farm, and given a coat of tar and feathers for alleged pro-German sentiments. He was then released and told to beat it for home.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: a local Wisconsin newspaper reporting matter-of-factly on vigilante violence. Purpose: to report (not condemn) the tarring and feathering of a man accused of 'pro-German sentiments.' Audience: local readers. Why it matters: the casual tone reveals how wartime conformity was enforced not only by statute but by community violence — the social dimension of the war's political change.

documents.text: Be it Resolved, by the War Industries Board, That the following agreement reached as a result of several conferences between a committee of the board and the American Iron and Steel Institute, be and the same is hereby ratified, confirmed, and approved, to become effective at once: Whereas, A careful study of the sources of supply in connection with the present and rapidly increasing direct and indirect war requirements for iron and steel products has convinced the War Industries Board of the necessity for (1) a strict conservation of the available supply of iron and steel products, on the one hand, and (2) the expansion of existing sources and the development of new sources of supply of iron and steel products, on the other hand.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: the War Industries Board, the federal agency coordinating wartime production. Purpose: to announce government direction of iron and steel supply — conservation, expansion, and allocation by federal authority with industry's cooperation. Audience: producers and the public. Why it matters: the document exemplifies the war's economic change — unprecedented federal management of private industry, a rehearsal for later twentieth-century economic intervention.

documents.text: Are we alone to ask and take the utmost that our women can give — service and sacrifice of every kind — and still say we do not see what title that gives them to stand by our sides in the guidance of the affairs of their nation and ours? We have made partners of the women in this war; shall we admit them only to a partnership of suffering and sacrifice and toil and not to a partnership of privilege and right?
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Wilson, personally lobbying the Senate for the women's suffrage amendment. Purpose: to argue that women's wartime service entitles them to full political partnership — 'a partnership of privilege and right.' Audience: U.S. senators. Why it matters: the war gave suffragists their decisive argument, and a wartime president's endorsement shows how the conflict accelerated the Nineteenth Amendment.

documents.text: [Descriptive entry — no excerpted text in the source: a 1919 cartoon playing on the 'melting pot' image in reverse, depicting the United States as unable to 'digest' undesirable newcomers, reflecting postwar nativist and anti-radical sentiment.]
documents.sourcing_note: Historical situation: drawn months after the armistice, amid the postwar Red Scare and a surge of nativism. Purpose: to express the view that the United States could not absorb ('digest') undesirable newcomers — radicals and immigrants cast as contaminants. Audience: readers of a mainstream Ohio daily. Why it matters: the cartoon captures the postwar reversal — wartime unity curdling into suspicion of foreigners and dissenters, the social backlash that limited the war's progressive legacies. (The book reprints the cartoon without a textual excerpt; this entry describes its argument from the title and historical context.)

documents.text: America's present need is not heroics, but healing; not nostrums, but normalcy; not revolution, but restoration; not agitation, but adjustment; not surgery, but serenity; not the dramatic, but the dispassionate; not experiment, but equipoise; not submergence in internationality, but sustainment in triumphant nationality. . . . The world needs to be reminded that all human ills are not curable by legislation, and that quantity of statutory enactment and excess of government offer no substitute for quality of citizenship.
documents.sourcing_note: Point of view: Harding, Republican presidential candidate, speaking to a business audience. Purpose: to promise a retreat from wartime government activism — 'not nostrums, but normalcy' — and to warn that legislation cannot cure all ills. Audience: businessmen and voters weary of war-era controls. Why it matters: the speech voices the political reaction that contained the war's changes, framing postwar America as a deliberate return to limited government.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Assess how far the Massachusetts Bay Colony differed from the Virginia colony between 1607 and 1754.
